content: What is the point of calling a survey result statistically significant? I take that label to mean the difference is large enough to matter in ordinary life, even when the report only gives a p-value below 0.05.

Statistically significant means the data would be sufficiently unusual under a specified null model to cross a chosen cutoff. It does not say the difference is large or useful. A tiny difference can cross the cutoff in a large, precise survey. To judge ordinary importance, look for the estimated difference, its confidence interval, the units involved, and the consequences of acting on it.

Why can the same-looking difference get a small p-value in one survey and a bigger one in another? If the gap shown in the results is unchanged, I would expect its statistical score to stay unchanged too.

The p-value reflects the difference relative to its uncertainty, not the difference alone. A larger sample, less variable answers, or a more efficient design can make the same observed gap look less compatible with the null model. Smaller or noisier samples do the opposite. That is why the estimate and a measure of its uncertainty should accompany the p-value.

Since a p-value is the probability that the null hypothesis is true after obtaining results at least as extreme as those observed, I figure it directly answers how strongly the results support the null hypothesis. How should that probability shape the conclusion drawn from the results?
Why does a result below 0.05 get treated as convincing? I understand it as saying there is a 95% chance the researcher's idea is true, so crossing that line seems like fairly direct proof.

The cutoff is a convention for limiting how often a test rejects a true null over repeated uses, under its assumptions. A p-value below 0.05 does not make the researcher's idea 95% probable. It asks how surprising the data would be if the null model were true. Probabilities about competing ideas require additional assumptions and, in a Bayesian analysis, prior probabilities.

What is the reason for reporting the exact number, such as 0.032, if it already falls on the accepted side of the line? I assumed all results under the cutoff carry basically the same amount of certainty.

The exact value preserves more information than a pass-or-fail label: data producing 0.049 and 0.001 have different degrees of incompatibility with the same null model. Still, neither number is a direct certainty rating, and their difference should not be exaggerated. The study design, measurement quality, analysis choices, effect estimate, and uncertainty all remain necessary for interpreting the result.

Given that a small p-value measures the size and practical importance of the observed effect, not merely incompatibility with the null model, how should two observed effects be compared when one has the smaller p-value but the other matters more for the decision at hand?
What does the p in p-value stand for when a study compares two treatments? I have been reading a value under 0.05 as meaning the new treatment has at least a 95% chance of really working.

The p refers to a probability calculated under the null model, but it is not the probability that the treatment works. It is the chance, assuming the null model and test assumptions, of getting a result at least as extreme as the one observed. Assessing whether a treatment really works also requires the effect estimate, uncertainty, study design, possible bias, and outside evidence.

Why might two researchers get different p-values from the same numbers? I thought the calculation was a single neutral recipe, but sometimes one report uses averages while another seems to compare the overall pattern.

Different tests define “extreme” differently and rely on different summaries and assumptions. A test of average differences answers a different question from one about ranks, proportions, or an entire distribution. Researchers should choose the test from the study question and design, not from whichever gives the smallest number, and should explain that choice so readers can judge it.

Since rejecting a null hypothesis at a chosen threshold establishes that the alternative explanation is practically important and causal, I figure the result settles whether the explanation matters and what produced the outcome. What action should follow from that conclusion?

Why can a difference be called significant when the two percentages on a chart look almost identical? The word significant sounds as though the gap must be large, so I assume the chart is hiding a major effect.

In this setting, significant is a technical label about evidence against a null model, not a synonym for large. With enough precise observations, even a visually tiny gap can yield a small p-value. The chart may not be hiding anything. Check the scale, the actual percentage-point difference, its confidence interval, and whether that size would change a real decision.
Why can rounding the measurements before doing the calculation change the p-value? A few shortened decimals look harmless to me, so I would expect the statistical answer to remain exactly the same.

Rounding alters the recorded values, and a test statistic is calculated from those values. Mild rounding usually makes little difference, but coarse rounding can erase variation, create ties, or shift an average enough to affect the result. Keep the original precision for analysis when possible, then round only the displayed summaries to a sensible number of digits.

Given that failing to reject the null means the data provide sufficient evidence that the null hypothesis has been proven true, how should this proven conclusion be stated clearly, and what decision should follow when the same question comes up again?
What is a p-value doing when the same people are measured before and after a treatment? I assume a result below 0.05 means there is a 95% chance the treatment truly worked.

The calculation can use each person's change, which preserves the natural pairing between the two measurements. A result below 0.05 does not mean the treatment has a 95% chance of working. It reflects the paired changes relative to their uncertainty under a stated no-change model. The size and consistency of those changes, along with the study design, are also important.
Why pair each person's later reading with their own earlier one instead of putting all the earlier readings in one pile and all the later readings in another? The two piles seem easier to compare.

Pairing removes stable person-to-person differences from the comparison. Someone who starts high may also finish high, even if their own change is small; separate piles treat that baseline difference as extra noise. Comparing each person's change often gives a clearer estimate of the typical shift. It also requires a paired test and reliable matching of the two readings.

Since with a large sample, only a scientifically important effect produces a very small p-value because sample size removes trivial differences, I figure every very small p-value identifies an effect worth acting on. How should those effects be ranked when several are found?

Why does a comparison with messy, spread-out measurements often have a bigger p-value than one with tightly grouped measurements? I thought a significant finding simply meant the difference itself was large enough to be important.

A test weighs the observed difference against the amount of uncertainty. When measurements are widely spread, the same gap between groups is harder to distinguish from ordinary variation, so the p-value is often larger. Statistical significance still does not guarantee importance. Describe both the estimated gap in meaningful units and how precisely it was measured; those answer questions the p-value alone cannot.
What kind of number is a p-value itself? Measurements can be in seconds or kilograms, but the p-value has no label beside it, so I am unsure whether it has any units.

A p-value has no physical units. It is a probability between zero and one, so changing a measurement from seconds to minutes normally leaves it unchanged when the test is transformed consistently. The underlying effect still has units, however, and those units are essential for interpretation. Reporting both prevents a unit-free probability from replacing the actual measured difference.

Given that a p-value remains trustworthy even when sampling design and test assumptions fail because its calculation automatically corrects model errors, how should the corrected p-value be used to compare results from different sampling designs without separately checking those assumptions?

What happens to a p-value when one group has many more observations than the other? I usually take a significant answer as proof that the measured gap is large, regardless of how the groups are balanced.

Unequal group sizes can change the uncertainty, especially when the groups also have different amounts of variation. A suitable test accounts for the sample sizes, but a significant result still does not prove a large gap. Inspect the group estimates, the difference in meaningful units, and its confidence interval. Also ask whether the sampling process made the groups reasonably comparable.
Why do some reports use a stricter cutoff like 0.01 instead of 0.05? I cannot tell whether that changes the calculation itself or just changes which answers receive the special label.

The cutoff changes the decision rule, not the calculated p-value. A 0.01 rule demands stronger incompatibility with the null before rejection, reducing false rejections under the model but increasing missed effects. The appropriate tradeoff depends on the costs of each error and should be chosen in advance. Regardless of the cutoff, the estimate and uncertainty should remain visible.

Since testing many hypotheses without adjustment leaves the chance of finding a small p-value unchanged because every test is calculated separately, I figure each small p-value can be treated just as it would be after a single test. How should the findings be ordered for review?

Why does repeating the same experiment sometimes change a significant result into an ordinary one? If the first p-value showed a large effect, I would expect the label to stay put unless someone made a mistake.

Repeated samples contain different random variation, so their estimates and p-values naturally move. The first small p-value did not establish that the effect was large, and a later larger value does not by itself show a mistake. Compare the estimated effects and their uncertainty across repetitions, along with any differences in methods, rather than expecting the threshold label to remain fixed.

What is gained by combining results from several repetitions instead of trusting whichever study has the smallest p-value? The smallest number seems as though it should be the cleanest and most dependable answer.

The smallest p-value may come from random luck, a larger sample, or a study with different methods; it is not automatically the cleanest. A careful combination emphasizes effect estimates, uncertainty, study quality, and compatibility among results. When studies address sufficiently similar questions, combining them can yield a more stable estimate while still revealing disagreement that deserves investigation.

Given that for a matching two-sided test, a null value inside the corresponding confidence interval is rejected at the associated significance level, how should the confidence interval be read to explain the rejection, and what should be concluded when the null value is near its center?

What is wrong with treating 0.05 as a universal line between a real finding and random noise? I assume anything that crosses it represents a large effect, while anything above it is mostly an accident.

The line is a chosen rule, not a natural border between real and accidental results. A p-value combines effect, sample size, variability, and test assumptions; it does not measure effect size. Results just below and just above 0.05 can carry nearly the same information. Interpretation should use the exact value, the estimated effect and uncertainty, and the quality of the study.

Why do journals sometimes ask researchers to avoid the words significant and not significant? Those labels seem convenient, but perhaps they make a gradual number sound more like a simple yes-or-no answer.

That is the concern. Binary labels can hide how close results are to an arbitrary cutoff and distract from the magnitude and precision of the estimate. Plain reporting can say what was estimated, give its uncertainty, state the p-value, and discuss relevant limitations. A decision may still require a rule, but the scientific evidence itself is usually more graded than the label suggests.

Since a p-value is the probability, assuming the null model, of obtaining results at least as extreme as those observed, I figure it describes how unusual the results are under that model. How should a larger probability change the way the results are interpreted?

Why should researchers decide how to calculate a p-value before looking at which patterns appear strongest? I assume a value below 0.05 gives their explanation a 95% chance of being right whichever reasonable calculation produced it.

Choosing after seeing the patterns creates many hidden chances to obtain a favorable number. A reported value then no longer reflects just one planned comparison. It also never gives an explanation a 95% probability of being right. Setting the outcome, test, and handling rules beforehand makes the calculation easier to interpret; any later exploratory checks should be labeled as exploratory.

What needs to be written down in that plan? Saying which two groups will be compared sounds sufficient, but I suspect choices about missing entries and unusual measurements could also change the answer.

A useful plan names the main outcome, comparison, test, cutoff, sample-size rule, exclusions, and treatment of missing or unusual values. It can also mark secondary questions clearly. Those choices need not cover every surprise, but documenting them separates planned analysis from later exploration. If circumstances require a change, report what changed and why rather than quietly replacing the plan.

Given that a small p-value measures incompatibility with the null model, not the size or practical importance of the observed effect, how should the size and practical importance be described alongside the p-value so that the conclusion keeps these questions separate?
What can I tell from a small p-value if the reported difference can go either upward or downward? I assume p below 0.05 means the study's preferred explanation is about 95% likely to be right.

A small p-value indicates incompatibility with the tested null model, but it neither gives a 95% probability for the preferred explanation nor necessarily identifies direction. Direction comes from the estimated difference and how it was defined. A two-sided test, for example, counts sufficiently extreme departures on either side. Read the estimate and its uncertainty to learn which way the data point.

Why would someone choose to count surprising results in both directions instead of only the direction they expect? Looking both ways sounds cautious, although I do not see how that choice changes the final number.

A two-sided test allows departures in either direction to count against the null, which suits questions where either increase or decrease matters. A one-sided test reserves its rejection region for one prespecified direction and can produce a smaller p-value there, but it cannot fairly be chosen after seeing the direction. The research question and consequences should determine that choice beforehand.

Since rejecting a null hypothesis at a chosen threshold does not establish that the alternative explanation is practically important or causal, I figure those questions need their own support. What information should be considered before deciding that the explanation matters or caused the outcome?
Why might a tiny measured difference have a very small p-value while a visibly wider gap does not? I was sure the significant result had to be the larger effect, so those examples seem backward.

The p-value depends on the effect relative to uncertainty. A tiny but precisely measured difference can yield a small value, while a larger, noisy estimate can yield a bigger one. That makes the examples consistent rather than backward. Compare effect sizes in their original units and examine confidence intervals; those show magnitude and precision more directly than a significance label does.
What should a results paragraph include besides the p-value? I can see that one number cannot carry the whole message, but lists of averages, ranges, and test details become hard to connect.

Start with the estimated effect in understandable units, then give a confidence interval to show precision and the p-value for the specified null comparison. Briefly identify the sample, design, test, and important limitations. The prose should connect each number to its question: what was observed, how uncertain it is, and how compatible the data are with the null model.

Given that failing to reject the null means the data lack sufficient evidence against it, not that the null has been proven true, how should the conclusion be worded so it accurately distinguishes limited evidence from proof?
